content: The document outlines various studies and reviews related to wheelchair provision services, their delivery models, and outcomes for users. Below is a professional interpretation of the content: 1. General Guidelines and Licensing: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published wheelchair provision guidelines, which include systematic reviews and data tables. These guidelines are available for non-commercial use, provided proper citation is given. Adaptations of the work must follow the same or equivalent Creative Commons licensing. WHO does not endorse specific organizations, products, or services, and the use of its logo is prohibited. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy of the translation. 2. Study Summaries: United Kingdom (Bray et al., 2014): A review of NHS wheelchair services for children under 18 with long-term mobility needs found that current services do not meet all needs. New Zealand (Graham et al., 2020): Tele-wheelchair assessments using video and audio communication were found to be feasible and effective. However, further research is needed to evaluate their long-term effectiveness and safety. Sweden (Hansen et al., 2004): A structured, active follow-up intervention for wheelchair users reduced accidents and improved satisfaction. Most wheelchairs develop defects over time, and users often cannot identify when action is needed. Research is needed to determine optimal follow-up intervals. USA (Hoenig et al., 2005): Multifactorial interventions involving expert therapists and structured assessments led to better wheelchair use and satisfaction compared to standard care. Afghanistan (Armstrong et al., 2007): Training programs for manual wheelchair users improved mobility, posture, and satisfaction. Adjustments to wheelchairs during the study were typical for maintaining functionality. Botswana (Divanoglou et al., 2019): A 7-day rehabilitation program for individuals with spinal cord injuries significantly improved physical independence. Community-based programs in low-resource settings can promote active, independent living. Indonesia (Toro et al., 2016): Wheelchairs provided using the WHO 8-step approach resulted in higher satisfaction and better quality of life compared to those on a waiting list. Mobility skills were identified as a confounding factor in measuring outcomes. Italy (Verza et al., 2006): An interdisciplinary approach to assistive device evaluation and prescription reduced wheelchair abandonment rates among individuals with multiple sclerosis. Kenya and the Philippines (Bazant et al., 2017): Training based on WHO guidelines improved wheelchair use outcomes. However, increased mobility may lead to unintended consequences, such as falls. Maintenance plans are essential. Zimbabwe (Visagie et al., 2016): Implementation of the WHO wheelchair guidelines in low-resource settings led to significant improvements in satisfaction and functionality, comparable to outcomes in high-resource settings. Ireland (Gowran et al., 2020): Ad-hoc wheelchair services negatively impacted users' independence and daily routines. Barriers during the provision process reduced perceived independence. Philippines (Leochico & Valera, 2020): Tele-rehabilitation sessions using low-cost technology were feasible and reduced travel-related fatigue and expenses. Participants reported improved perceptions of care. Croatia (Štefanac et al., 2018): Inclusion in the wheelchair selection process and skills training improved safety and satisfaction. However, many participants were excluded from parts of the process, negatively affecting their outcomes. USA (Suzuki et al., 2000): Clients at a wheelchair seating clinic were satisfied with services but highlighted the need for better follow-up on equipment orders and fittings. 3. Key Findings: Structured follow-ups and training improve wheelchair safety, satisfaction, and functionality. Telehealth and community-based programs are promising in low-resource settings but require further research. Economic evaluations and cost-effectiveness studies are lacking in this field. User involvement in the wheelchair selection process enhances satisfaction and safety. Maintenance and repair plans are critical to ensuring long-term wheelchair usability. 4. Conclusion: The studies emphasize the importance of structured, user-centered approaches to wheelchair provision. They highlight the need for ongoing research, particularly in low-resource settings, to optimize service delivery and improve outcomes for wheelchair users.
